findings.headline: Outgoing wires are priced near the top of your cohort.
findings.body: At $30.00, your outgoing domestic wire fee runs 50% above the $20 median of 43 comparable credit unions — the 91st percentile. Deposited-item returns follow the same pattern: $30.00 against a $20 median (80th percentile among 25 peers). Two exception fees, each $10 over median, together define your schedule's most exposed edge.

findings.headline: Your NSF fee sits above a falling market.
findings.body: Your $30 NSF fee lands at the 83rd percentile of 66 comparable credit unions, against a $25 median. A quarter of those peers now charge $20 or less, and the low end of the cohort has reached zero as institutions retire returned-item fees under sustained scrutiny. The market under this fee is moving down, not up.

findings.headline: You are below market on member service fees — quietly.
findings.body: Card replacement ($10.00 vs a $25.00 median, 38th percentile across 94 peers) and paper statements ($1.00 vs $2.75, 25th percentile) are priced well under most comparable credit unions. That is a genuine member-friendly position, but today it earns you nothing, because no one has been told.

exec_narrative: Net position: Lockport Schools & Community Federal Credit Union runs a split schedule. Exception and penalty fees — outgoing wires, deposited-item returns, NSF — cluster in the top quartile of the cohort, while everyday service fees like card replacement and paper statements sit meaningfully below market. Three categories (non-network ATM, monthly maintenance, overdraft) do not appear in the published schedule at all, which limits comparability for members and analysts alike. The exposure is asymmetrical: the high exception fees draw attention while the below-market service fees earn no credit. The three findings above are the agenda for a one-hour pricing conversation.

callouts.title: Outgoing domestic wire — $30.00
callouts.body: A $30 outgoing wire fee sits above the 75th percentile of your cohort, and wires are used disproportionately by your most engaged members — home closings, tuition payments, family transfers. At $10 over median the revenue is modest but the position is conspicuous. This line deserves a deliberate decision: hold with a rationale, or move toward the $20 center of the market.

callouts.title: Deposited item return — $30.00
callouts.body: This fee charges a member because someone else's check failed — a charge members consistently experience as unfair, since the failure is not theirs. At $30 you sit at the top edge of the cohort, $10 over the median. Fees that punish members for third-party behavior are exactly the category regulators and comparison sites highlight first.

callouts.title: NSF / returned item — $30.00
callouts.body: The industry-wide retreat from NSF fees has reached small credit unions: your cohort's median is $25 and falling, with the low end already at zero. A $30 NSF fee is not yet an outlier, but it is on the wrong side of the trend line. Whether the answer is a cut, a cap, or a documented rationale, this fee should be a decision rather than a default.

callouts.title: Service fees — below market, unmarketed
callouts.stat: Card replacement $10.00 vs $25.00 median (P38) · Paper statement $1.00 vs $2.75 median (P25)
callouts.body: Two everyday member fees run well under your cohort. If deliberate, they belong in your member communications — 'lower service fees than most comparable credit unions' is a claim your peers' own published schedules substantiate. If not deliberate, they represent margin available without touching a single headline fee. Either way, the current state — below market and invisible — is the one position that earns nothing.

context_narrative:
Two currents define the fee landscape your schedule competes in. First, the retreat from NSF: the largest institutions have largely eliminated returned-item fees, and the pressure has migrated down-market — visible in your own cohort, where a quarter of comparable credit unions now charge $20 or less and the low end has reached zero. Second, published fee schedules have become public documents in a real sense: scraped, compared, and surfaced in searches, which converts every outlier line into a small reputational bet. Regulatory attention to so-called junk fees has only sharpened the comparison.

Small community credit unions compete on something the money-center institutions cannot buy: relationship and trust. That makes fee-schedule coherence unusually valuable at your scale — members forgive a fee they understand and resent one that feels arbitrary. The highest-leverage moves here are surgical: bring the two or three top-of-cohort exception fees toward the middle, publish the categories currently missing from your schedule, and actively tell the below-market service-fee story you already own.
